title: How orbit speed works
short: Gravity bends a moving spacecraft into an orbit.
body: A spacecraft in a circular orbit keeps falling around the world. Gravity supplies its inward acceleration; it is not cancelled by an outward force in an inertial frame. This equation assumes a spherical central body and a circular orbit.
symbols: v: speed (m/s); G: gravitational constant; M: mass of the central body (kg); r: distance from its centre (m), not altitude.
caption: Your EM0508 Topic 1 slides, page 13 · Singapore Polytechnic / Wall-Pie, 2024.
source: NASA Basics of Space Flight; supplied EM0508 slides

title: Why distant orbits take longer
short: A wider orbit usually takes longer to complete.
body: For two objects orbiting the same much heavier body, the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. An ellipse and a circle with the same semi-major axis have the same period in the two-body model.
symbols: T: period (s); a: semi-major axis (m); G: gravitational constant; M: mass of the central body (kg).
caption: Your EM0508 Topic 4 slides, page 6 · Singapore Polytechnic / Wall-Pie, 2024.
source: NASA Basics of Space Flight; supplied EM0508 slides

title: How a rocket pushes
short: A rocket throws gas one way to move the other way.
body: A rocket carries its propellants. The nozzle speeds up the hot gas as it leaves. Rockets work in a vacuum; they do not need air to push against. The pressure term depends on the pressure outside the nozzle.
symbols: F: thrust (N); ṁ: mass flow (kg/s); vₑ: exhaust speed (m/s); pₑ and pₐ: exit and ambient pressures (Pa); Aₑ: exit area (m²).
caption: Your EM0508 Topic 6 slides, page 4 · Singapore Polytechnic / Wall-Pie, 2024.

title: Gravity on the Moon
short: You weigh about one sixth as much on the Moon.
body: Surface gravity is about 1.62 m/s². Your mass stays the same. The game uses lunar gravity for jumps; moving a heavy rover still takes force.
symbols: W: weight (N); m: mass (kg); g: gravity (m/s²). A 60 kg person weighs about 97 N on the Moon.
caption: An Apollo bootprint in lunar soil · NASA · NASA catalogue date: 2021-04-21

title: No wind on the Moon
short: The Moon has almost no air, so there is no wind.
body: Its extremely thin exosphere cannot carry ordinary wind or sound. Rocket exhaust can kick up dust, which follows ballistic paths rather than billowing like a cloud in air. Music is a soundtrack; suit and cabin sounds are heard through equipment or pressurised air.
caption: The Moon from Orion · NASA · NASA catalogue date: 2026-04-06

title: A very long lunar day
short: Sunrise to sunrise takes about 29.5 Earth days.
body: The Moon rotates in about 27.3 Earth days, but its motion around the Sun makes its solar day about 29.53 Earth days. Near the poles, local terrain changes how long a place stays lit or in shadow. Game time is sped up.

title: Ice in dark polar places
short: Some deep polar shadows can hold water ice.
body: Scientists have detected water ice in permanently shadowed regions near the lunar poles. It is not an everywhere-ready water supply. Finding, digging and processing useful deposits remain engineering challenges.
caption: Lunar polar water-ice observations · NASA · 2017-12-08

title: Artemis I and II: around the Moon
short: Artemis I and II did not land on the Moon.
body: Artemis I tested SLS and Orion without a crew in 2022, including lunar orbit and return to Earth. Artemis II carried four astronauts on a lunar flyby in April 2026. Orion carries crew through deep space and returns them to Earth. The surface game is a separate future-training scenario.
caption: Earth setting behind the Moon, seen from Orion · NASA · NASA catalogue date: 2026-04-06

title: Why the Moon lander looks different
short: A lunar lander needs engines, not a parachute.
body: SLS launches Orion from Earth. A Human Landing System is a separate vehicle for travelling between lunar orbit and the surface. An HLS-inspired Starship has no need for the atmospheric reentry fins and Earth-return heat shield shown on a Mars/Earth Starship concept. Exact designs can change. Our model illustrates the role; it is not a flight-certified blueprint.

title: Real science and game rules
short: Real facts guide the game; distances and time are shortened.
body: Planet facts and images have sources. Terrain is a training landscape, not a surveyed landing site. Resource yields, mission lengths, construction recipes, radiation effects and spacecraft animations are simplified. NASA API keys provide access to particular services; they do not generate models or make every image live.

title: The map-sized world limit
short: Detailed terrain follows the area shown by your minimap.
body: The minimap spans 240 game metres. Map-sized detail loads the tiles touching a 120 m radius around you. Tiles use a small boundary margin so their edges do not expose gaps. A coarse horizon remains beyond it. Your mission state and buildings are not deleted when terrain unloads.
source: Game design; not a NASA measurement

title: Jumping and sprinting on the Moon
short: Less gravity means a longer, higher jump.
body: The game keeps lunar gravity at 1.62 m/s². Walking is 2 m/s; hold Shift to sprint at 4 m/s. The tuned jump launch speed is 2.9 m/s, giving about 2.6 m of rise and 3.6 seconds in the air on level ground. These speeds are game choices, not astronaut performance measurements. A bulky pressurized suit, equipment and technique affect real jumps. With the same launch speed, a lunar jump is about six times higher than on Earth.
symbols: h: rise above takeoff (m); v₀: upward launch speed (m/s); g: gravity (m/s²); t: time back to the same height (s). Ignores air resistance; assumes level landing.
source: NASA reduced-gravity locomotion research; game movement settings

title: NASA Moon and spacecraft models
short: Our flyby Moon uses NASA LRO imagery and topography.
body: On computers and tablets the flyby loads NASA’s original topographic GLB and 8192 × 4096 texture unchanged. Phones automatically load a separate Lite derivative; choose Full quality in Settings to load the original on a phone too. The Orion crew capsule uses NASA’s detailed STL; its service module and arrays are illustrative game geometry. The surface lander is an HLS-inspired training design. NASA’s astronaut and Space Exploration Vehicle models are also used. The walkable terrain is procedural with a NASA LOLA-derived distant horizon; it is not an exact survey of a landing site. Assets load once and are reused; nearby terrain uses bounded chunks.
source: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / LRO; NASA 3D Resources
